Empirical Research Plan  

------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy  
------------------------------------------------------------
Primary design: Sharp Regression-Discontinuity Design (RDD) at the Democratic vote-share majority threshold in mayoral elections.

Rationale  
• The treatment (party of the elected mayor) switches deterministically at the 50 percent vote-share cutoff.  
• Close elections create quasi-random assignments of partisan control, neutralising un-observed city characteristics that simultaneously influence policy and electoral outcomes.  
• The panel structure lets us extend the single-shot RDD into a “RD-event study”: we estimate instantaneous effects (year t) and dynamic effects in years t+1, t+2, …, conditional on the same quasi-experiment.  
• Alternative designs (plain DID with party changes, IV, etc.) would rely on stronger functional-form or exogeneity assumptions.  

------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control  
------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
• Treat = 1 if the Democratic candidate wins the mayoral election, 0 if the Republican wins.

Running variable & cutoff  
• Running variable m = (Democratic two-candidate vote share – 50).  
• Cutoff at m = 0.

Sample window (bandwidth)  
• Main bandwidth: |m| ≤ 5 percentage points (≈ 9–10 percent of the sample).  
• Robustness: Imbens–Kalyanaraman optimal bandwidth; ±2.5 pp and ±7.5 pp windows.

Event timing  
• t = 0: fiscal year that begins after inauguration (to avoid budget overlap).  
• Dynamic outcomes traced for up to four years (typical mayoral term length).  

Counterfactual  
• Cities in which the Republican just barely wins serve as the control group; they are expected to be identical in expectation except for the party of the mayor.

------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Continuity of potential outcomes at the cutoff.  
 City characteristics and unobservables must change smoothly with m.  
 Plausibility: Fraud or precise manipulation of city-wide elections is difficult; existing evidence in U.S. elections supports continuity.

A2. No precise sorting/manipulation of the running variable.  
 Testable via McCrary density test; plausibility reinforced by decentralised vote counting.

A3. Stable unit treatment value (no cross-city spillovers within narrow margins).  
 Plausible because most metropolitan-area interactions occur across a set of municipalities whose own elections are not mechanically tied to the focal city’s razor-thin result.

A4. Consistency of party affiliation coding.  
 The constructed Dem/Rep indicator must reflect the actual ideological alignment.  
 Plausible given archival work, but we will perform sensitivity checks excluding ambiguous cases.

A5. Correct bandwidth choice and functional-form specification.  
 Local linear/quadric regressions with robust bandwidth choice mitigate model dependence.

------------------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats and Remedies  
------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Manipulation of the margin (fraud, recounts).  
 Remedy: McCrary density test; reassess using precinct-level recount data where available; drop recount elections as a robustness check.

T2. Covariate imbalance close to cutoff (e.g., incumbency advantage).  
 Remedy: Balance tests on pre-election covariates (population, income, crime trends, previous spending shares). If imbalance appears, control flexibly for the covariate interacted with a polynomial in m.

T3. Post-treatment compositional changes (migration, annexation).  
 Remedy: Restrict outcomes to per-capita measures; for crime, use rates per 1,000 residents; check robustness to excluding cities with annexations >5 % population change during term.

------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline  
------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# Load packages
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(fixest)      # fast high-dimensional fixed effects
library(rdrobust)    # RD estimation
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Read data -------------------------------------------------------------
elections <- read_csv("elections.csv")       # one row per election
finance   <- read_csv("finances.csv")        # city-year panel
crime     <- read_csv("fbi_crime.csv")

# 2. Construct running variable & treatment -------------------------------
elections <- elections %>%
  mutate(dem_margin = dem_vote_share - rep_vote_share,
         dem_win    = ifelse(dem_margin > 0, 1, 0),
         margin_pct = dem_margin)            # already in p.p.

# Keep contested Dem-vs-Rep elections
elections_dr <- elections %>% filter(dem_rep_race == 1)

# 3. Merge outcomes to election fixed window ------------------------------
# Assume mayor takes office in year+1 of election; attach term years
term_years <- elections_dr %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  do({
    city  <- .$city_id
    y0    <- .$election_year + 1
    data.frame(city_id = city,
               election_id = .$election_id,
               dem_win = .$dem_win,
               margin_pct = .$margin_pct,
               year = y0:(y0+3))           # four-year window
  })

panel <- term_years %>%
  left_join(finance, by = c("city_id", "year")) %>%
  left_join(crime  , by = c("city_id", "year"))

# 4. MAIN SPECIFICATION: local linear RD on first post-election fiscal year
main_rd <- rdrobust(y = panel$total_exp_percap[panel$year == panel$election_year+1],
                    x = elections_dr$margin_pct,
                    c = 0,
                    h = 5,  # 5 pp bandwidth
                    p = 1)

summary(main_rd)

# 5. EVENT STUDY within RD window (|m|<=5) -------------------------------
panel_es <- panel %>%
  filter(abs(margin_pct) <= 5) %>%
  mutate(rel_year = year - (election_year + 1))   # 0,1,2,3

est_es <- feols(total_exp_percap ~ i(rel_year, dem_win, ref = -1) | city_id + election_year,
                data = panel_es, cluster = ~city_id)

etable(est_es)

# 6. ROBUSTNESS: alternate bandwidth (IK) -------------------------------
bw_ik <- rdbwselect(y = panel$total_exp_percap[panel$year == panel$election_year+1],
                    x = elections_dr$margin_pct)$bws[1]

rd_ik <- rdrobust(y = panel$total_exp_percap[panel$year == panel$election_year+1],
                  x = elections_dr$margin_pct,
                  c = 0, h = bw_ik, p = 1)

summary(rd_ik)
```

------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results  
------------------------------------------------------------
Given inter-jurisdictional competition and voter homogeneity, I expect:  
• Total size of government: statistically indistinguishable (~ ±1 % of mean per-capita spending).  
• Composition: Democrats shift spending marginally toward redistributive or public-employee-intensive categories (e.g., +2 pp share to fire + parks; –2 pp to police).  
• Crime rates: near zero average difference (⇐ policing budget effect roughly offset by selection of chief).  
• Electoral advantage: Incumbent’s party gains roughly +3 pp in subsequent mayoral election vote share in close-win cities.

------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (RDD)  
(C1) No manipulation at cutoff ………………… 1  
(C2) Covariate continuity verified ……………… 1  
(C3) Correct functional form/bandwidth ……… 0.5 (bandwidth choice still subjective)  
(C4) SUTVA / no spillovers ……………………… 0.5 (possible metro spillovers)  
(C5) Outcome measured consistently ………… 1  

Total: 4/5 – design looks credible but still warrants robustness tests.
